glynac.text: Users take GlyNAC in longevity-minded appearance circles in the hope that restoring glutathione slows ageing and keeps skin looking younger. The small trials measured glutathione and ageing markers in older adults, not wrinkles or skin appearance, so the skin link is speculative.

alpha-ketoglutarate.text: AKG is taken by people in longevity circles who hope slowing biological ageing will show up as younger skin and fewer wrinkles. Research is preliminary and focused on ageing markers; effects on visible skin ageing in people are untested.

caffeine-topical.text: Users apply caffeine creams and serums under the eyes to reduce puffiness and dark circles, usually before photos or events. Vasoconstriction explains a short-lived effect; small studies exist for under-eye products, while claims about facial fat or body fat are anecdotal.

hesperidin.text: Hesperidin is a citrus flavonoid that users take hoping to improve under-eye circulation and reduce dark circles and puffiness. It has been studied for venous and capillary complaints in the legs, not under-eye appearance, so this use rests on extrapolation.

dandelion-extract.text: Users take dandelion tea or extract as a herbal diuretic to shed water weight and reduce facial puffiness, sometimes before a shoot or event. Evidence for a meaningful diuretic effect in people is weak and limited to small studies; appearance outcomes are untested.

potassium.text: Looksmaxxers raise potassium intake, usually through food, to offset sodium and reduce water retention and facial bloat. Potassium's role in fluid balance is well established, but whether it changes facial puffiness has not been directly studied; forum claims about ratios and powders are anecdotal.

furosemide.text: Some users misuse this prescription diuretic off-label to drop water weight for a leaner or less puffy look before events or photos. It is studied for oedema, not cosmetic use; the effect is fluid loss rather than fat loss, and the appearance use is based on anecdote.

whitening-strips.text: Users apply peroxide strips to lighten tooth colour for a brighter smile, often as the first whitening step. Peroxide bleaching is well studied for whitening; forum debates concern sensitivity, gum effects and non-peroxide or charcoal alternatives, which have less evidence.

whitening-gel-trays.text: Users wear gel trays, custom or over-the-counter, to whiten teeth with peroxide, with posters claiming more even coverage than strips. Peroxide whitening is well studied; direct comparisons of tray types and long-term enamel effects are less certain, and forum claims vary.

chain: Peroxide gel plus blue LED light
led-whitening-kit.text: Users buy LED whitening kits as a home version of in-office light-assisted whitening, hoping the light speeds or boosts results. The peroxide gel is the studied active ingredient; evidence that the LED adds anything is limited.

electric-toothbrush.text: Users switch to electric brushes for cleaner, healthier-looking teeth and gums and fresher breath. Powered brushes are studied for plaque and gum health; whitening claims are mostly about reducing surface stain and are less well supported.

water-flosser.text: Users add water flossers to clean between teeth and keep gums healthy so the smile looks better and breath is fresher. Studies have examined gum bleeding and plaque; comparisons with string floss and safety concerns are debated on forums.

tongue-scraper.text: Users scrape the tongue to reduce coating and bad breath, which matters for close-up social presence. Studies show a short-lived reduction in breath odour and tongue coating; claims about the oral microbiome or diet-related breath are mostly anecdotal.

clear-aligners.text: Users wear clear aligners to straighten teeth and correct bite, and some hope for subtle facial-structure benefits such as palate width. Tooth movement is well studied; claims about jaw or facial-skeleton change are limited and debated, and larger skeletal problems are generally described as needing other treatment.

chain: Less tooth wear and jaw strain
bruxism-night-guard.text: Users wear night guards to stop grinding from flattening teeth and to ease jaw strain, which they link to keeping teeth and facial symmetry intact. Splints are studied for protecting teeth; effects on facial appearance are untested.

jaw-exerciser.text: Users chew against silicone devices hoping for a sharper jawline and reduced double chin. The masseter can be trained, but forum posters note bigger muscles may widen the lower face; effects on definition or chin fat are largely untested.

mastic-hard-gum.text: Users chew mastic or hard gum to give the jaw muscles resistance work in hope of a more defined jawline. Jaw-muscle growth from chewing is plausible, but evidence for jawline appearance is anecdotal, and posters also raise joint-strain concerns.

mouth-tape.text: Users tape their mouths at night to encourage nasal breathing, claiming better sleep, fresher breath and in some forums forward jaw and midface development. Sleep and snoring effects have limited study; claims of adult facial-bone remodelling are unsupported.

mewing-appliances.text: Users buy palate plates and mouthpieces alongside mewing, hoping to remodel the jaw, chin and midface. Orthotropic theory is contested; adult skeletal change without orthodontic treatment is undocumented, and the real effect in teens is described as small.

chain: Red light absorbed by skin cells
red-light-led-mask.text: Users wear red light masks to smooth fine lines, even tone, calm acne and improve texture. It is one of the better-studied consumer device categories, though trials vary by device; claims about hair loss or focus and household red lamps are weaker.

blue-light-acne-device.text: Users apply blue light devices to acne-prone skin to cut inflammatory breakouts. Clinic-strength blue light has been studied for mild to moderate acne; evidence for lower-powered home devices is thinner.

at-home-fractional-laser.text: Users try low-energy handheld fractional lasers for fine lines, texture, mild scars and uneven tone. Clinic fractional lasers are well studied; evidence for home versions is more limited and varies by device.

rf-skin-tightening-device.text: Users use home radiofrequency devices to firm skin and sharpen the jaw and neck contour. Clinic RF is studied for modest tightening; evidence for lower-power home devices is more limited.

microcurrent-device.text: Users apply microcurrent as a non-invasive facelift, often before events, for a lifted look and less puffiness. Small studies suggest short-lived effects; claims about masseter pain, ATP or anxiety treatment are weakly supported.

multi-head-facial-tool.text: Users buy all-in-one facial devices to combine light, microcurrent and massage for fine lines and puffiness. The LED component has more supporting data than the microcurrent head, and trials of the combined devices are limited.

chain: Deeper removal of oil and debris
sonic-cleansing-brush.text: Users cleanse with sonic brushes to remove makeup and sebum more thoroughly than hands, aiming for clearer, brighter skin and fewer breakouts. Studies suggest better debris removal; acne and scar effects are less studied.

chain: Blade removes dead cells and peach fuzz
dermaplaning-razor.text: Users shave the face with a single blade to remove peach fuzz and dead skin for an instant smoother, brighter look. Evidence is mostly clinical and anecdotal; improved product absorption and scar benefits are less studied.

derma-roller-home.text: Users roll the face with fine needles to soften acne scars and texture and fine lines, and some try it on brows. Professional microneedling has trial data; home rollers use shorter needles with weaker evidence, and infection risk is debated.

gua-sha-stone.text: Users stroke gua sha stones across the face to de-puff and sculpt the jaw and cheeks, and some hope for fewer wrinkles. Evidence for lasting facial change is limited; the effect is generally described as temporary fluid movement.

ice-roller.text: Users roll a chilled head over the face in the morning to cut puffiness and calm skin before events. Cold's short-term de-puffing effect is plausible; lasting benefits for texture or wrinkles are untested.
